steps.html:
A locked bathroom, a fireman's helmet, and a mother who says none of it happened. Two texts about how early memory works, and the small grammatical difference between remembering to do something and remembering doing it.

  • Read two texts about memory and compare them
  • Use verbs followed by -ing and by the infinitive
  • Know which verbs change meaning with each form
  • Write an account of an early memory

steps.title: The bathroom, the ladder and the helmet
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 149 words

I was two. I can recall it very clearly, which everybody tells me is impossible, and I have stopped arguing about it.

I remember being locked in the bathroom. I do not remember getting there. My mother tried to open the door from outside, failed, and decided to call the fire department, which arrived within about four minutes and enjoyed itself enormously.

One of the firemen climbed a ladder and broke the window. I remember his helmet slipping over his eyes, and I remember him saying something I could not understand. I have no recollection of being carried out.

My mother refuses to accept most of this. She admits calling the fire brigade and denies that anybody broke a window. She says the door was opened with a screwdriver in under a minute, and that I was asleep. Somebody is remembering wrongly, and neither of us intends to give way.

steps.title: What is the disagreement between the writer and her mother?
options: Whether the fire brigade was called at all.
Whether a window was broken and how the door was opened.
Whether the writer was in the bathroom.
steps.answer: Whether a window was broken and how the door was opened.
steps.why: The mother 'admits calling the fire brigade and denies that anybody broke a window'.

steps.title: Why nobody remembers being three
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 147 words

Almost nobody has a reliable memory from before the age of about three and a half. Psychologists call it childhood amnesia, and they have stopped explaining it as simple forgetting.

The current account is that very young children do form memories, and manage to keep them for a while, but fail to store them in a way that survives. From about seven, children begin to analyse events more clearly and to place them in time. Before that, a memory has no date and no order, and tends to fade.

This explains something that puzzles people. Adults often claim to remember an event from the age of two, and describe it in detail. Frequently the detail comes from a photograph they have seen, or a story the family enjoys telling. The memory is real. What is remembered is the retelling.

steps.title: Answer the questions.
steps.prompt: What is the current explanation for childhood amnesia?
options: Young children do not form memories at all.
They form them and keep them briefly, but fail to store them in a way that survives.
The memories are stored but cannot be reached.
steps.answer: They form them and keep them briefly, but fail to store them in a way that survives.
steps.why: 'They have stopped explaining it as simple forgetting.'

steps.title: Which form follows which verb
steps.html:
Three lists to know, and one small group where the choice changes the meaning.

Some verbs are followed by -ing: enjoy, admit, deny, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, involve, imagine, keep, practise, risk, consider. She admits calling the fire brigade.

Some are followed by the infinitive with to: agree, decide, refuse, manage, offer, promise, hope, fail, seem, tend, appear, choose, intend, learn. She decided to call the fire department.

Some take either with no real change: begin, start, continue, like, love, hate, prefer. It began to fade / began fading.

And then the group that matters. With remember, forget, stop, try, regret, go on, the two forms mean different things.

Remember doing = the memory of a past action. Remember to do = not forgetting an obligation. I remember being locked in (I have the memory). I remembered to lock it (I did not forget).

Stop doing = end the activity. Stop to do = pause in order to do something else. Try doing = experiment with it. Try to do = attempt something difficult. Regret doing = be sorry about the past. Regret to say = be sorry about the news you are giving.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts.

I have stopped arguing about it.
Ended the activity.

I remember being locked in the bathroom.
The memory of a past event.

I do not remember getting there.
Same use, negative.

She tried to open the door.
Attempted something difficult.

She decided to call the fire department.
Decide takes the infinitive.

The fire brigade enjoyed itself enormously.
Not a verb pattern — but enjoy always takes -ing.

She admits calling the fire brigade.
Admit + -ing.

She denies that anybody broke a window.
Deny takes -ing or a that clause, never the infinitive.

Neither of us intends to give way.
Intend + infinitive.

They have stopped explaining it as simple forgetting.
Ended that explanation.

Children begin to analyse events more clearly.
Begin takes either form.

Adults often claim to remember an event from the age of two.
Claim + infinitive.

steps.title: Two sentences, one word apart
steps.html:
1. The verb is remember, and the two forms are not interchangeable.
  2. I remember locking the door. The locking happened first; the remembering came afterwards. This is a memory.
  3. I remembered to lock the door. The remembering happened first; the locking followed. This is an obligation you did not forget.
  4. The test: put the two actions in order. If the action came before the remembering, use -ing. If it came after, use to.
  5. The same order test works for the others. She stopped arguing — the arguing was already happening. She stopped to argue — the arguing came after the stopping.

steps.title: You are going to write about an early memory.

options.label: A memory you now suspect came from a photograph
Something you remember only because it was retold

steps.title: Write your account.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least three verbs followed by -ing and at least three followed by the infinitive, and use remember both ways.
steps.placeholder: I was … , and I can recall …
steps.html:
• Open with your age and how clear the memory is.
  • Say what you remember, using <i>remember + -ing</i>.
  • Say what you do not remember, using the same form.
  • Bring in somebody who disputes it, using <i>admit</i>, <i>deny</i> or <i>refuse</i>.
  • Close with what you now think, using <i>stop</i> or <i>suspect</i>.

Useful language

  • I can recall it very clearly, which everybody tells me is impossible.
  • I remember … -ing. I do not remember … -ing.
  • I have no recollection of …
  • My mother refuses to accept … / admits …-ing / denies …-ing
  • My memory of it has begun to fade.
  • What is remembered may be the retelling.
steps.modelHtml:
The blue gate

I was three, or possibly four, and I can recall it very clearly, which I am told means almost nothing.

I remember standing at a blue gate that came up to my shoulder, and I remember being lifted over it rather than through it. I do not remember arriving, and I have no recollection whatsoever of the journey home.

My father denies that the gate was ever blue. He admits painting it, twice, and insists on green both times. He also refuses to accept that I could have been lifted over anything, since he had a bad back that year and avoided carrying us at all.

I have stopped arguing. I now suspect I am remembering a photograph — there is one, and in it the gate is dark enough to be either colour.
